explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while.” Many people were coming and going, and the apostles did not even have time to eat. I think that sounds like a week where a nap feels like a vacation. Rest was the invitation, friend.

Prayer is a good thing, so I see why you picked it. But the word in Jesus' invitation is “rest.” He says, “…let us rest for a while.” Nothing in that verse mentions praying. I think a quiet spot to catch their breath sounds kind after all that coming and going.

Celebrating sounds fun, but that's not the word. Jesus says, “…let us rest for a while.” The verse mentions no party at all. I think a quiet place with no crowd and no confetti sounds just right after a day with no time to eat.

explanations.answer: Run there on foot and get there first
explanations.explanation: They saw the boat leave and recognized who was in it. Then they ran together on foot from all the towns and arrived before Jesus and the apostles (Mark 6:33). Think about that. People on foot beat a boat. I can't even beat my own oven timer to the oven.

explanations.answer: Wait on the shore for the boat to come back
explanations.explanation: Nobody sits and waits on the shore here. The text says they ran together on foot from all the towns. They didn't wait for the boat to return. They arrived before it did.

explanations.answer: Go back home to their own towns
explanations.explanation: That would've given the apostles their quiet day. But the people headed the other way. They ran on foot from all the towns and arrived before Jesus and the apostles. Home was the last place on their minds, friend.
That's not what happens. When Jesus stepped ashore and saw the large crowd, He had compassion on them (Mark 6:34). He didn't send anyone away. Instead, He began to teach them many things.

Right, He doesn't send them away. Jesus stepped ashore, saw the large crowd, and had compassion on them. The text says they were like sheep without a shepherd. So instead of leaving, He began to teach them many things.

That's what the text says. Jesus saw they were like sheep without a shepherd, and He began to teach them many things. I think that tells us a lot about how He saw the crowd. He had compassion, and then He started teaching.

explanations.answer: Pray with them by the sea
explanations.explanation: That's a nice picture, but it's not what Mark says here. The text says He began to teach them many things. Praying with them isn't mentioned in this verse. His compassion showed up as teaching.

explanations.answer: Sing psalms with them on the shore
explanations.explanation: I can picture a whole crowd singing, but the text doesn't say that. It says He had compassion because they were like sheep without a shepherd. Then He began to teach them many things. Teaching is the answer, friend.

Yes, that's what they say. The disciples tell Jesus, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” They point out that it's a desolate place and the hour is already late. Jesus answers with something they didn't see coming.

It's true, actually. The disciples do say it. They tell Jesus, “Dismiss the crowd so they can go to the surrounding countryside and villages and buy themselves something to eat.” That's how Mark 6:36 puts it.

explanations.answer: Far too little to go around
explanations.explanation: Jesus tells them to go and see how many loaves they have. After checking, they come back with five loaves and two fish. Remember, they'd just asked about spending two hundred denarii on bread for everyone. Five loaves is a long way from that.

Not quite. After checking, the disciples report five loaves and two fish. They'd already wondered about spending two hundred denarii to feed the crowd. Five loaves and two fish is nowhere close to just enough for that many people.

I wish my pantry worked that way. But the disciples check and find only five loaves and two fish. Remember, they'd just talked about spending two hundred denarii on bread. What they found wasn't more than enough.

explanations.answer: Sit down in groups on the green grass
explanations.explanation: Jesus directs them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass. They sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. Not a word about the size of the food yet. I think there's something calm about grass and orderly groups.

explanations.answer: Head off to the villages in groups
explanations.explanation: Close, but that was the disciples' idea. They wanted the crowd to go to the surrounding countryside and villages to buy something to eat (Mark 6:36). Jesus goes another way. He has the people sit in groups on the green grass.

Lining up is a fair guess for a hungry crowd. But the text says Jesus directed them to have the people sit in groups on the green grass. They sat in groups of hundreds and fifties. The shore isn't mentioned.
That's right. Taking the five loaves and the two fish, Jesus looked up to heaven and spoke a blessing. Then He broke the loaves. The blessing comes first, friend.
It's actually true. The text says Jesus took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, and spoke a blessing. Only then did He break the loaves. I almost got a little teary at that part.

Yes, that's it. After breaking the loaves, Jesus gave them to His disciples to set before the people. He also divided the two fish among them all. So the disciples were the ones putting the food in front of the crowd.

It's true, actually. The text says Jesus broke the loaves and then gave them to His disciples to set before the people. The two fish were divided among them all. The disciples got to carry the food out.
That's the word. They all ate and were satisfied. That means a whole crowd, not just the front row. And that was from five loaves and two fish.
You'd expect that from five loaves and two fish. But the text says they all ate and were satisfied. Nobody walked away hungry. Not one person in that whole crowd.
That's a creative guess, but the text doesn't say it. It says they all ate and were satisfied. Everybody ate, and everybody had enough. Satisfied is the word.

The disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish. Remember, they started with only five loaves and two fish. After everyone ate and was satisfied, there was far more left than they began with. My leftovers after a long baking day fit in a single cookie tin.

That would be a normal amount of leftovers. But the text says the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish. That's a lot more than a handful of crumbs, friend. And it was left over from five loaves and two fish.

Half a basket would already be a surprise. But Mark says the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces of bread and fish. That's twelve full baskets, not half of one. All of it was left after everyone had eaten.
